questions.scenario: A team of five building a new wallet product proposes 12 microservices from day one because 'that's how big fintechs do it'.
questions.question: What is the best advice?
options: Use one service per database table
Start with a modular monolith with clear module boundaries, and extract a service when there's a concrete reason such as independent release cadence or very different load
Build all 12 services now so they never need splitting later
Split by technical layer: a controller service, a service service and a repository service
questions.explanation: Services buy independence and scaling at the cost of network calls, distributed data and operations. A small team should pay that cost only where it buys something.

questions.scenario: Onboarding, Payments and the Ledger all use the word 'account', each with different fields and rules. One shared `Account` class now has 60 fields.
questions.question: What does DDD suggest?
options: Rename the class to AccountDto
Add more optional fields to the shared class
Treat them as separate bounded contexts, each with its own Account model, translating at the boundaries
Store the account as JSON so every team can add fields
questions.explanation: A bounded context is where one model and vocabulary apply consistently. Different meanings of the same word signal different contexts.

questions.scenario: ITL Pay must integrate with NIBSS NIP, whose ISO message fields and codes don't match the team's transfer model.
questions.question: Which context-map relationship fits?
options: Conformist: use NIP's message classes everywhere in the code
A shared kernel containing NIBSS's full schema
Shared database with NIBSS
An anti-corruption layer that translates NIP messages into the team's own model at the edge
questions.explanation: An ACL keeps an external, awkward model from leaking into your domain; only the adapter knows NIP's format.

questions.scenario: A `Customer` aggregate contains all the customer's accounts, cards and transactions. Two simultaneous transfers on different accounts of the same customer conflict on an optimistic lock.
questions.question: What is the design problem?
options: Transactions should be stored in the session
Transfers should be processed one at a time for the whole bank
The aggregate is too large; make Account its own aggregate and reference others by id
Optimistic locking should be turned off
questions.explanation: Aggregates should be small consistency boundaries. One transaction changes one aggregate; others are referenced by id.

questions.scenario: The Accounts and Transfers services both read and write the `account` table in one shared database 'to keep things simple'.
questions.question: What is the consequence?
options: It enables two-phase commit automatically
Better performance with no downsides
They can't be changed or deployed independently: a schema change in one breaks the other, so it's effectively one service with two deployments
None, as long as both use JPA
questions.explanation: Database per service is what makes services independent. Others use the owner's API or events.

questions.scenario: A Spring Modulith project has modules `account` and `notification`. `ApplicationModules.of(App.class).verify()` fails after a change in notification.
questions.question: What most likely happened?
options: Notification now uses a type from a sub-package of account (an internal type) or the modules depend on each other in a cycle
Module names must be plural
Spring Modulith doesn't support events
The test needs a running database
questions.explanation: By default a module's API is the public types in its base package; sub-packages are internal. verify() also rejects cycles.

questions.scenario: Every release of your 'microservices' requires deploying Accounts, Transfers and Ledger together, and one request makes a synchronous chain of six calls.
questions.question: What is this called?
options: A modular monolith
A distributed monolith: the costs of services without their independence
Event sourcing
A service mesh
questions.explanation: If services must be released together and fail together, the boundaries are wrong or the coupling too tight.

questions.scenario: You must replace a 15-year-old payments monolith without a big-bang cut-over.
questions.question: Which approach fits?
options: Freeze all features for two years
Copy the monolith's database into each new service and let them all write to it
The strangler fig: route one capability at a time to new code behind a gateway, and delete the old path when it has no traffic
Rewrite everything and switch over on a weekend
questions.explanation: Incremental replacement keeps risk small and lets you prove each piece in production.
